ranking.one_line: Nine strip-shaped samples of spacecraft materials were set alight inside an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit to see whether they burn more or less readily than in NASA's standard ground flammability test; silicone and Nomex would not burn in weightlessness, while a cotton-fibreglass fabric and thick acrylic burned but with flames that stopped growing.

key_findings.claim: No flame spread on silicone in microgravity. None of the four silicone sheets (0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm concurrent; 0.37 mm opposed; 20 cm/s air, about 22.1% O2; the PSI table lists sample 2-1 at about 21.5% while the published Table I (NTRS 20170008805) gives about 22.1%) propagated. After the 9.2 s, 80 W igniter switched off, a tiny gas-phase flame remained briefly, did not spread and went out. Burn time was 'insignificant' and microgravity burn length about 0 for all four.

Silicone was less flammable in microgravity than in the 1-g test. In 1-g tests on matching samples, the 0.27 mm silicone burned completely with accelerating upward spread, the 0.61 mm burned on average 7.6 cm of 30 cm (1.2 mm/s) and the 1.03 mm did not burn. The 0.37 mm sheet burned completely downward at 0.6 mm/s. Published 1-g Test 1 minimum oxygen concentrations (MOC; the term used by the cited source) for silicone are 18% (0.25 mm), 20% (0.61 mm) and 22% (1.00 mm), so the roughly 22.1% O2 flight atmosphere was at or above the 1-g MOC for every thickness. The investigators conclude silicone flammability in microgravity is reduced compared with 1 g, at least at 20 cm/s. This was unexpected: cellulose and PMMA experience suggested that a material that burns upward in 1 g would also burn in microgravity at moderate flow.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts burned small fabric strips, plastic spheres and slabs, and wax candles in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS to see whether solids burn more readily without gravity than in the Earth-based test NASA uses to approve materials, and whether a puff of nitrogen puts the flames out.

key_findings.claim: In opposed flow in microgravity (2-cm-wide SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric, ISS air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), the flame reached steady spread within seconds of each flow change. Spread rate rose with flow to a maximum at about 10-15 cm/s and fell at higher speeds.

The same SIBAL fabric cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) spread in 1 g air: it ignites, then extinguishes, because the buoyant flow exceeds the blow-off limit. In microgravity at about 9-10 cm/s opposed flow it burned steadily over the whole sample. For this fabric and geometry, it is more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g, which supports the BASS hypothesis.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station photographed small gas flames burning from a tube into a gentle stream of air, to see how flames lift off, hold on and make soot without gravity and to provide test cases for computer models of flames.

key_findings.claim: Microgravity made a sooting methane flame larger, sootier and cooler. For a 100% CH4 flame on the 3.23 mm nozzle (mean fuel velocity 46 cm/s, nominal coflow 18 cm/s), the microgravity flame was taller and wider than its 1-g counterpart. Its peak soot volume fraction was about 8 times higher, and its peak soot temperature about 200 K lower because of the larger radiative loss.

The model predicted flame shape and soot location but not the microgravity soot increase. The sectional soot model reproduced the 1-g to microgravity change in flame shape and the shift of soot to the wings. It gave the right order of magnitude for 1-g soot but did not capture the eightfold rise in microgravity. The investigators suspect the optically thin radiation assumption (no reabsorption).

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames surrounded by a gentle co-flowing air stream were burned on the Space Station, from very diluted near-extinction flames to very sooty ones, to give computer models clean, buoyancy-free benchmark data; the sooty flames held several times more soot than on Earth and diluted flames survived at lower fuel concentrations.

key_findings.claim: SLICE precursor (N2-diluted CH4, mole fraction 0.4-1.0, mean inlet velocity 23-90 cm/s): luminous flame length is proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow in both 1 g and microgravity, microgravity flames are noticeably longer, dilution has negligible effect on shape once normalised by methane flow, and buoyancy narrows 1 g flames through radially inward convection near the flame front.

Campaign scope from the PSI table: 344 flames on 32 test days across three ISS rounds (methane Nov 2017-Feb 2018, 130 flames; ethylene May-Sept 2018, 162 flames; 'improved coflow tests' Feb-Mar 2021, 52 flames), with 2 to 18 flames per day.

ranking.one_line: A repeat of the first large spacecraft fire experiment, with the air blowing a little faster, to see how ventilation speed changes how fast a large sheet of fabric burns in an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit.

key_findings.claim: Concurrent burn (S1) at about 25 cm/s and 21.2-21.0% O2, near 1 atm: the flame spread over about 84 cm of the 40.6-cm-wide sheet at an average 2.3 mm/s, burning for about 300 s (investigators' table; 320 s in the ASGSR slides). In 1 g the same configuration burns completely with an accelerating flame. Together with Saffire-I, the investigators conclude that concurrent spread over this thin fabric in microgravity reaches a steady rate and a limiting flame length.

Opposed burn (S2) at about 25 cm/s: the flame spread into the flow at 0.98 mm/s over about 10 cm in 60 s. This fabric does not spread downward in 1 g (burn length ~0). At 25 cm/s the concurrent flame spread 2.3 times faster than the opposed flame, against 1.4 times at 20 cm/s in Saffire-I.

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames on the Space Station were placed in a strong electric field between the burner and a metal mesh; the field drags the flame's natural ions and the gas around them, creating an adjustable 'ion wind' that can reshape, compact, de-soot or stabilise the flame with no buoyancy present.

key_findings.claim: First buoyancy-free mapping of ion-wind effects on flames: ISS tests ran March-November 2018 (20 test days, 219 flames) with methane and ethylene flames on coflow and gas-jet burners in fields of either polarity up to 10 kV, giving data on ion current and flame response without the confounding natural convection present in all ground tests.

In microgravity the voltage-current characteristic of methane coflow flames shows a distinct peak ion current at saturation, where the flame is most compact; beyond the saturation peak the current falls along a parabolic branch, unlike the 1 g plateau.

ranking.one_line: University at Buffalo researchers built and tested fast computer models of flames spreading over solid fuels in weightlessness, checking them against Space Station burning tests, as a step toward predicting which spacecraft materials can burn at which oxygen levels and air speeds.

key_findings.claim: Building the flamelet manifolds from 1-D flames with a quasi-coupled fuel surface boundary (rather than a fixed fuel inlet) is critically important for capturing the spatial variation of mixture fraction along a pyrolysing fuel surface.

The coupled radiative FGMs reproduce the wide range of chemical states (intermediate species) of the detailed 2-D solution in most of the flow, but differ near the flame attachment (leading-edge) location, where flame-wall interaction before the fuel starts to burn and curved flame structure are not represented by 1-D flamelets.

notes: Score = weighted mean of four components in [0, 1]: conditions (closeness of the nearest test to the scenario's O2, pressure and flow), material (fuel-phase transfer), pillar and evidence strength. Weights and scales are in fif/api.py and docs/methods.md; they are a judgement, shown so it can be argued with.

A distance of 1 means one scale step away: 3 points of O2, 15 kPa or 10 cm/s. A condition that was not recorded counts as far away as the farthest investigation that did record it (at least 2 steps); cabin-air experiments without logged O2 or pressure are placed at the nominal cabin atmosphere (listed in conditions_assumed_cabin_air).

A condition with no per-test value is read from the investigation's range (conditions_from_range or conditions_assumed_cabin_air; range and origin in condition_ranges); a wide range lowers the conditions score by 20%. A value shown for a column in a test's `not_measured` is the middle of a narrow range, not a reading of that test.
No PSI combustion test was run at partial gravity (0.38 g). The gravity component only rewards investigations that compare microgravity with 1 g, which brackets partial gravity.

fuel_phase weights the ranking, it does not filter it: an investigation on another fuel phase keeps its place with a lower material component and `phase_match` false. `nearest_test` is always a liquid-fuel test (null when the investigation ran none); the test of another phase that its conditions score and distance come from is in `nearest_test_other_phase`.

ranking.one_line: Single drops of methanol and heptane were burned floating freely on the Space Station in air thinned with nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium, to find how little oxygen still lets a fuel burn in weightlessness and how well these gases put flames out; it also discovered that heptane drops keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame dies.

key_findings.claim: Limiting oxygen index in O2/N2: about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for n-heptane droplets. NASA describes the LOI found as significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted; the 2012 FLEX overview states microgravity flames burned at as much as 2-3 percent less oxygen (the source does not say whether relative or absolute). Consistent with this, the PSI table lists methanol tests that burned 5-11 s and extinguished at 0.12 O2 (8 tests) and heptane tests at 0.13 O2 that burned only 1.0-1.5 s with extinction diameter about equal to the initial diameter (transient burning below the LOI).

Carbon dioxide as suppressant: dispersing CO2 into 1 atm air raised the LOI to about 0.14 for methanol (0.14 O2/0.56 N2/0.30 CO2) and about 0.17 for heptane (0.17 O2/0.63 N2/0.20 CO2), i.e. roughly 30% and 20% CO2 by volume were needed to prevent quasi-steady burning of these fuels. The authors attribute the higher LOI to CO2's larger heat capacity (lower flame temperature) and its radiative participation. The PSI table shows methanol still burning 3.4-5.9 s at 0.14 O2 with 0.36 CO2, and heptane at 0.17 O2/0.20 CO2 extinguishing after 1.6-1.9 s with d_ext/d0 = 0.97.

ranking.one_line: The follow-on to FLEX burned single drops and pairs of drops of practical-fuel ingredients and fuel mixtures (octanes, heptane, decane, alcohols) on the Space Station to give engine and fire modellers clean benchmark data, and showed that the 'cool flames' found in FLEX occur for many normal-alkane fuels.

key_findings.claim: Cool-flame (second-stage) burning after hot-flame radiative extinction occurs for several n-alkanes, not only heptane: n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets in O2/N2/CO2 and O2/He/N2 at 0.5, 0.7 and 1 atm (14-25% O2) showed quasi-steady low-temperature burning, cool-flame extinction at a finite diameter and vapour-cloud formation, while smaller droplets burned to completion or disrupted. Cool-flame extinction diameters of the three alkanes followed a trend resembling their ignition delay times.

n-Decane at 0.5 atm in O2/N2: a 4.03 mm droplet in air burned with K = 0.41 mm2/s in the hot-flame stage (visible extinction at ~14.6 s) and 0.33 mm2/s in the cool-flame stage, whose end was marked by a drop in the narrowband radiometer signal; at 25% O2 a 3.79 mm droplet avoided radiative extinction and micro-exploded at 26 s (K = 0.52 mm2/s); at 17% and 14% O2 hot/cool K were 0.31/0.27 and 0.29/0.25 mm2/s with earlier extinctions.

ranking.one_line: A flat gas burner on the Space Station imitated small burning patches of plastics and liquids in still air, showing that such flames can burn steadily for minutes without any air flow when oxygen is raised to about 26.5% or more, but go out within tens of seconds at 21%.

key_findings.claim: Small (25 mm) emulated condensed-fuel flames burned quasi-steadily for minutes in quiescent microgravity, with no air flow and no flame spread; more than half of round-1 tests (59 analysed ignitions) burned at least 2 and up to 5 minutes, and ~29 flames reached an apparently steady state for 120 s or more before shutdown.

Oxygen threshold for the 25 mm ethylene/N2 flames tested: all flames in 21% O2 (by volume) self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas steady flames were observed at nominal 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2. NASA's summary places the self-extinction boundary at roughly 25% O2. This is a threshold for these burner conditions (flow rates, sizes), not a material flammability limit.

ranking.one_line: Ground-commanded tests on the ISS burned ethane, propane and butane on a pea-sized porous sphere, both normally (fuel out of the sphere into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere) and inside-out (an oxygen-rich stream of up to 85% O2 out of the sphere into a fuel-filled chamber), and found the first spherical 'cool flames' of gaseous fuel.

key_findings.claim: Fifteen spherical cool diffusion flames of a gaseous fuel were observed, the first such observation. All followed radiative extinction of a hot flame, after a dark interval of 0.7-1.1 s. The cool flames of four tests in June 2021 (21174 C3, C4, C6, F1) were quasi-steady for about 14 s and disappeared when the fuel flow stopped; in one test the radiometer and burner temperature were steady enough to suggest the cool flame would have lasted indefinitely. The ten cool flames of tests 21291 A1 and C1 instead ended by re-igniting into hot flames.

Cool flames formed in a narrow window only: normal (not inverse) flames, n-butane (not ethane or propane) at 30% in N2 in the burner stream, flowing at 0.75-1.5 mg/s into 0.385-0.399 ambient O2 at 2.03 bar (about 203 kPa). Burner temperature also had to be above 515 K. None were seen below about 0.4 O2, below 2 bar, or for any inverse flame, including those fed with 85% O2.

ranking.one_line: On the space station, small ball-shaped flames of ethylene gas were burned for minutes around a porous sphere, either as fuel blowing into oxygen-rich air or as oxygen blowing into a fuel atmosphere, to learn when such flames make soot and when they go out.

key_findings.claim: At about 1 atm, every ethylene spherical flame that extinguished radiatively did so at a peak temperature of about 1130 K. The reactant mass flux through the flame sphere at extinction was about 0.2 g/m^2/s of fuel for normal flames and 0.68 g/m^2/s of oxygen for inverse flames. This held across normal flames with ambient X_O2 0.20-0.38, burner X_fuel 0.13-1, total flow 0.6-12.2 mg/s and T_ad 2000-2800 K, and inverse flames with ambient X_C2H4 0.08-0.12, burner X_O2 0.40-0.85, 2.3-11.3 mg/s and T_ad 2080-2590 K.

At constant burner flow, the normal ethylene flames at 1 atm grew monotonically after ignition while their peak gas temperature generally fell. Burn times were 28-336 s. Radiative extinction occurred when the growing flame's radiative loss approached its chemical heat release. Just before total extinction, many flames entered an oscillatory mode, partially extinguishing and re-forming with growing amplitude.

ranking.one_line: On the Space Station, small pieces of common spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lamp wick) were overheated without burning, and the size of the smoke particles was measured to find out what kind of smoke detector would reliably catch an early spacecraft fire.

key_findings.claim: Fresh (unaged) smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity was sub-micrometre in number terms. Final-report values (geometric mean / count mean / diameter of average mass, nm; sigma_g): Kapton 80/105/179, 2.08; lamp wick 186/227/341, 1.89; silicone rubber 189/257/472, 2.18; Teflon 170/205/297, 1.84.

Holding the smoke for 720 s raised all mean sizes and narrowed the distribution, consistent with coagulation. Geometric mean diameter rose to 155 nm (Kapton, x1.9), 258 nm (lamp wick, x1.4), 352 nm (silicone, x1.9) and 228 nm (Teflon, x1.3). Diameter of average mass rose by 28-49%, to 267-606 nm, and sigma_g fell to 1.81-1.83 for all four materials. During aging the P-Trak number count fell substantially while DustTrak mass stayed nearly constant, which indicates coagulation with little wall loss.

ranking.one_line: Fuel droplets about 4 mm across were burned in a sealed chamber on the ISS to study 'cool flames': invisible, low-temperature flames (roughly 700-900 K) that keep a droplet burning after its normal hot flame has gone out.

key_findings.claim: With pure n-dodecane in air (21% O2, balance N2), droplets of about 3.8-4.7 mm at 0.5-1.25 atm burned first with a hot flame. The flame went out by radiative extinction after about 10-14 s (up to 17 s), with the droplet at about 2.9-4.3 mm. Quasi-steady cool-flame burning usually followed, often ending with a large vapour cloud. Not every test shows this: FLEX-1207 to 1210 have no cool-flame extinction diameter, the FLEX-1207 comment notes no large vapour cloud, and the FLEX-1222 comment says the flame burned to completion. The cool-flame burning-rate constant (0.31-0.43 mm^2/s) was about the same as the hot-flame value (0.30-0.52 mm^2/s).

For n-dodecane in air the cool-flame extinction diameter falls steeply with pressure. It was 1.73-1.92 mm at 0.5 atm (50.7 kPa; 5 tests), 0.68-1.14 mm at 0.75 atm (76 kPa; 5 tests), mostly 0.26-0.85 mm at 1 atm (101 kPa; one outlier of 2.97 mm in FLEX-1251), and 0-0.39 mm at 1.25 atm (127 kPa). At 2-5 atm most droplets left no measurable residual droplet (recorded as 0 mm). The investigators note that simplified chemistry predicts these diameters less well as pressure rises.

pressure_kpa.note: reported for film tests; about 1 atm overall

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station burned tiny gas jets in a gentle, adjustable air stream and turned the fuel up until each flame just started to give off smoke, to learn how air flow and burner size control soot release when there is no gravity.

key_findings.claim: Laminar smoke points exist for non-buoyant co-flowing jet flames, contrary to Glassman's 1988 prediction. On the ISS, 52 smoke points (final-report table: 6 ethylene, 6 propane, 20 propylene, 13 for 75% and 7 for 50% propylene; the same report's closing remarks say 55) were found at 0.41-1.6 mm burners and 5.4-65 cm/s co-flow. All smoke-point flames were attached, with Re 36-788.

For a given fuel and burner, raising the co-flow velocity lengthens the smoke point, even though at fixed fuel flow it shortens the luminous flame. Example (pure propylene, 1.6 mm burner, smoke-point review sheet): L_SP rose from about 14.0 mm at u_a = 9.1 cm/s to 25.7 mm at 51.4 cm/s. The investigators attribute this to decreased residence times and radiative losses as co-flow velocity increases.

The 0.37 mm sheet burned completely downward at 0.6 mm/s. Published 1-g Test 1 minimum oxygen concentrations (MOC; the term used by the cited source) for silicone are 18% (0.25 mm), 20% (0.61 mm) and 22% (1.00 mm), so the roughly 22.1% O2 flight atmosphere was at or above the 1-g MOC for every thickness. The investigators conclude silicone flammability in microgravity is reduced compared with 1 g, at least at 20 cm/s. This was unexpected: cellulose and PMMA experience suggested that a material that burns upward in 1 g would also burn in microgravity at moderate flow.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station photographed small gas flames burning from a tube into a gentle stream of air, to see how flames lift off, hold on and make soot without gravity and to provide test cases for computer models of flames.

key_findings.claim: Microgravity made a sooting methane flame larger, sootier and cooler. For a 100% CH4 flame on the 3.23 mm nozzle (mean fuel velocity 46 cm/s, nominal coflow 18 cm/s), the microgravity flame was taller and wider than its 1-g counterpart. Its peak soot volume fraction was about 8 times higher, and its peak soot temperature about 200 K lower because of the larger radiative loss.

The model predicted flame shape and soot location but not the microgravity soot increase. The sectional soot model reproduced the 1-g to microgravity change in flame shape and the shift of soot to the wings. It gave the right order of magnitude for 1-g soot but did not capture the eightfold rise in microgravity. The investigators suspect the optically thin radiation assumption (no reabsorption).

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames surrounded by a gentle co-flowing air stream were burned on the Space Station, from very diluted near-extinction flames to very sooty ones, to give computer models clean, buoyancy-free benchmark data; the sooty flames held several times more soot than on Earth and diluted flames survived at lower fuel concentrations.

key_findings.claim: SLICE precursor (N2-diluted CH4, mole fraction 0.4-1.0, mean inlet velocity 23-90 cm/s): luminous flame length is proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow in both 1 g and microgravity, microgravity flames are noticeably longer, dilution has negligible effect on shape once normalised by methane flow, and buoyancy narrows 1 g flames through radially inward convection near the flame front.

Campaign scope from the PSI table: 344 flames on 32 test days across three ISS rounds (methane Nov 2017-Feb 2018, 130 flames; ethylene May-Sept 2018, 162 flames; 'improved coflow tests' Feb-Mar 2021, 52 flames), with 2 to 18 flames per day.

ranking.one_line: On the space station, gas fuels (hydrogen, methane, ethylene, diluted with nitrogen or helium) were fed out of a small porous ball into still oxygen-containing gas to make nearly perfect spherical flames, to see how such flames grow, and how they go out when the fuel supply is too small or when the flame becomes so large that it loses too much heat by radiation.

key_findings.claim: For nitrogen-diluted ethylene in air (20% C2H4/80% N2 fuel stream, ~21% O2, ~1 atm), a flow of 3 cc/s produced a quasi-steady spherical flame that lasted until the automated system stopped it at the 250 C burner limit. Radiative extinction of growing spherical diffusion flames, predicted computationally but never conclusively seen in 2.2 s or 5 s drop towers or on parabolic aircraft, turned out to be a common event on the ISS. The investigators list it first among the flight's initial surprises and discoveries.

ranking.one_line: On the ISS, small pieces of five common spacecraft materials were overheated (without burning) to make smoke, and instruments measured how big the smoke particles were and whether the Shuttle and ISS smoke detectors would have noticed them.

key_findings.claim: Unaged baseline smoke at 8 cm/s was sub-micrometre for every material. Kapton had geometric mean diameter Dg = 0.047 um, count mean 0.062 um and diameter of average mass 0.106 um. Teflon had Dg 0.093 um and D_avm 0.173 um, lampwick 0.103 and 0.271 um, silicone 0.152 and 0.468 um, and Pyrell 0.177 and 0.377 um. The geometric standard deviation was 2.03-2.38. Typical runs had a few million particles per cm3 and 2-15 mg/m3. (These are the final-report values; the appended 2012 paper gives slightly different numbers, e.g. Kapton Dg 0.042 um.)

Aging the smoke for 720 s in the chamber made the particles larger and the distribution narrower. D_avm rose from 0.106 to 0.169 um (Kapton), 0.271 to 0.401 um (lampwick), 0.468 to 0.628 um (silicone) and 0.377 to 0.529 um (Pyrell), and sigma_g fell to 1.67-1.96. Teflon was the exception: Dg did not grow (0.093 to 0.080 um) and sigma_g widened to 2.34. Number counts fell by a factor of 1.7-2.7 over about 800 s. This agreed with coagulation theory within about 20% for number and 4% for D_avm, but sigma_g fell more than twice as much as predicted.

ranking.one_line: NASA lit a 94-cm-long sheet of cotton-fibreglass fabric inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS, the first large fire deliberately set in orbit, to see whether a fire in microgravity keeps growing or settles to a steady size.

key_findings.claim: In concurrent flow at about 20 cm/s and 21.7% O2 (falling to 21.5%) near 1 atm, the flame over the 40.6 cm x 94 cm SIBAL sheet reached a steady state: it spread at a constant average 1.8 mm/s, and the flame length reached a plateau of about 40 mm. It burned about 84 cm of the 94 cm sheet during the 420 s allotted. On Earth the same configuration (upward burning) consumes the whole sample with an accelerating flame. This answers the main Saffire question: a large concurrent fire in microgravity, under forced ventilation, need not keep growing.

The opposed-flow flame (spreading into the 20 cm/s flow, ~21.5% O2) burned the remaining ~10 cm of fabric in about 70 s at an average 1.3 mm/s, with a flame length of about 24 mm. In 1 g this fabric does not spread downward (burn length ~0). So for this material, opposed-flow spread is possible in microgravity at a cabin-like ventilation speed but not on Earth. The concurrent flame spread about 1.4 times faster than the opposed flame.

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames on the Space Station were placed in a strong electric field between the burner and a metal mesh; the field drags the flame's natural ions and the gas around them, creating an adjustable 'ion wind' that can reshape, compact, de-soot or stabilise the flame with no buoyancy present.

key_findings.claim: First buoyancy-free mapping of ion-wind effects on flames: ISS tests ran March-November 2018 (20 test days, 219 flames) with methane and ethylene flames on coflow and gas-jet burners in fields of either polarity up to 10 kV, giving data on ion current and flame response without the confounding natural convection present in all ground tests.

In microgravity the voltage-current characteristic of methane coflow flames shows a distinct peak ion current at saturation, where the flame is most compact; beyond the saturation peak the current falls along a parabolic branch, unlike the 1 g plateau.

ranking.one_line: A repeat of the first large spacecraft fire experiment, with the air blowing a little faster, to see how ventilation speed changes how fast a large sheet of fabric burns in an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit.

key_findings.claim: Concurrent burn (S1) at about 25 cm/s and 21.2-21.0% O2, near 1 atm: the flame spread over about 84 cm of the 40.6-cm-wide sheet at an average 2.3 mm/s, burning for about 300 s (investigators' table; 320 s in the ASGSR slides). In 1 g the same configuration burns completely with an accelerating flame. Together with Saffire-I, the investigators conclude that concurrent spread over this thin fabric in microgravity reaches a steady rate and a limiting flame length.

Opposed burn (S2) at about 25 cm/s: the flame spread into the flow at 0.98 mm/s over about 10 cm in 60 s. This fabric does not spread downward in 1 g (burn length ~0). At 25 cm/s the concurrent flame spread 2.3 times faster than the opposed flame, against 1.4 times at 20 cm/s in Saffire-I.

ranking.one_line: Before flying a smoke-measuring experiment, NASA checked on the Space Station that a commercial particle counter, which normally relies on gravity to recycle its alcohol, still counted particles correctly in weightlessness, and in doing so made the first measurement of how dusty the Station air is.

key_findings.claim: The modified P-Trak worked in microgravity. In all sessions (2005 and 2006, runs of about 8-39 min) it showed no alcohol flooding, optics obscuration, nozzle clogging or error codes. Readings rose from zero into the middle of the range and returned to zero on HEPA zero checks. This was the main failure mode the condenser modification was meant to prevent.

The P-Trak tracked a high-concentration aerosol (Velcro test, 4 Mar 2005). When the crew repeatedly separated Velcro at the inlet, it rose to several readings above 30,000 particles/cm3 (logged maximum 45,400) and fell back in a logical way. The DustTrak also responded but stayed below 10% of its range. These readings could not be tied quantitatively to individual Velcro separations.

ranking.one_line: Yale researchers re-analysed Space Station photographs of sooty ethylene flames and ran detailed computer models to find out why flames in weightlessness make so much more soot than on Earth, concluding that the models mainly get the flame temperature wrong.

key_findings.claim: Simulations of both burner configurations reproduce the established microgravity trends for sooting ethylene-air coflow flames: at 0 g the flame is longer, broader and more diffuse, temperatures are lower, and soot levels and gas residence times are higher than at 1 g. No numerical values were available in the sources read.

For the smaller ACME burner flame, the gravity effects (lengthening, cooling, extra soot) were significantly diminished compared with the Yale burner flame, so flame size matters when transferring 1 g soot behaviour to microgravity.

ranking.one_line: A computer simulation of smoke forming from a hot, vapour-releasing sample in a slow air stream shows that, without gravity, smoke particles can grow larger than on Earth, which matters for how spacecraft smoke detectors are designed.

key_findings.claim: At the SAME flow speed (8 cm/s), the Earth-gravity size distribution sampled 26 L0 downstream (Case 1EG) has a single maximum near 5 um and no particles larger than about 40 um. The microgravity distribution (Case 1MG) is bimodal, with maxima near 5 um and 30 um, and a small fraction of particles approaching 100 um.

In Earth gravity, buoyancy deflects hot DBP vapour toward the cool (300 K) upper wall. The resulting peak nucleation rate is about 1e14 m-3 s-1, against about 1e12 m-3 s-1 in microgravity, where nucleation occurs only around the edge of the wake. Number densities near the upper wall approach 1e12 m-3, so terrestrial smoke has far more particles below 5 um.

ranking.one_line: University at Buffalo researchers built and tested fast computer models of flames spreading over solid fuels in weightlessness, checking them against Space Station burning tests, as a step toward predicting which spacecraft materials can burn at which oxygen levels and air speeds.

key_findings.claim: Building the flamelet manifolds from 1-D flames with a quasi-coupled fuel surface boundary (rather than a fixed fuel inlet) is critically important for capturing the spatial variation of mixture fraction along a pyrolysing fuel surface.

The coupled radiative FGMs reproduce the wide range of chemical states (intermediate species) of the detailed 2-D solution in most of the flow, but differ near the flame attachment (leading-edge) location, where flame-wall interaction before the fuel starts to burn and curved flame structure are not represented by 1-D flamelets.

notes: Score = weighted mean of four components in [0, 1]: conditions (closeness of the nearest test to the scenario's O2, pressure and flow), material (fuel-phase transfer), pillar and evidence strength. Weights and scales are in fif/api.py and docs/methods.md; they are a judgement, shown so it can be argued with.

A distance of 1 means one scale step away: 3 points of O2, 15 kPa or 10 cm/s. A condition that was not recorded counts as far away as the farthest investigation that did record it (at least 2 steps); cabin-air experiments without logged O2 or pressure are placed at the nominal cabin atmosphere (listed in conditions_assumed_cabin_air).

A condition with no per-test value is read from the investigation's range (conditions_from_range or conditions_assumed_cabin_air; range and origin in condition_ranges); a wide range lowers the conditions score by 20%. A value shown for a column in a test's `not_measured` is the middle of a narrow range, not a reading of that test.
No PSI combustion test was run at partial gravity (0.38 g). The gravity component only rewards investigations that compare microgravity with 1 g, which brackets partial gravity.

fuel_phase weights the ranking, it does not filter it: an investigation on another fuel phase keeps its place with a lower material component and `phase_match` false. `nearest_test` is always a liquid-fuel test (null when the investigation ran none); the test of another phase that its conditions score and distance come from is in `nearest_test_other_phase`.

ranking.one_line: A flat gas burner on the Space Station imitated small burning patches of plastics and liquids in still air, showing that such flames can burn steadily for minutes without any air flow when oxygen is raised to about 26.5% or more, but go out within tens of seconds at 21%.

key_findings.claim: Small (25 mm) emulated condensed-fuel flames burned quasi-steadily for minutes in quiescent microgravity, with no air flow and no flame spread; more than half of round-1 tests (59 analysed ignitions) burned at least 2 and up to 5 minutes, and ~29 flames reached an apparently steady state for 120 s or more before shutdown.

Oxygen threshold for the 25 mm ethylene/N2 flames tested: all flames in 21% O2 (by volume) self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas steady flames were observed at nominal 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2. NASA's summary places the self-extinction boundary at roughly 25% O2. This is a threshold for these burner conditions (flow rates, sizes), not a material flammability limit.

ranking.one_line: Ground-commanded tests on the ISS burned ethane, propane and butane on a pea-sized porous sphere, both normally (fuel out of the sphere into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere) and inside-out (an oxygen-rich stream of up to 85% O2 out of the sphere into a fuel-filled chamber), and found the first spherical 'cool flames' of gaseous fuel.

key_findings.claim: Fifteen spherical cool diffusion flames of a gaseous fuel were observed, the first such observation. All followed radiative extinction of a hot flame, after a dark interval of 0.7-1.1 s. The cool flames of four tests in June 2021 (21174 C3, C4, C6, F1) were quasi-steady for about 14 s and disappeared when the fuel flow stopped; in one test the radiometer and burner temperature were steady enough to suggest the cool flame would have lasted indefinitely. The ten cool flames of tests 21291 A1 and C1 instead ended by re-igniting into hot flames.

Cool flames formed in a narrow window only: normal (not inverse) flames, n-butane (not ethane or propane) at 30% in N2 in the burner stream, flowing at 0.75-1.5 mg/s into 0.385-0.399 ambient O2 at 2.03 bar (about 203 kPa). Burner temperature also had to be above 515 K. None were seen below about 0.4 O2, below 2 bar, or for any inverse flame, including those fed with 85% O2.

ranking.one_line: On the space station, small ball-shaped flames of ethylene gas were burned for minutes around a porous sphere, either as fuel blowing into oxygen-rich air or as oxygen blowing into a fuel atmosphere, to learn when such flames make soot and when they go out.

key_findings.claim: At about 1 atm, every ethylene spherical flame that extinguished radiatively did so at a peak temperature of about 1130 K. The reactant mass flux through the flame sphere at extinction was about 0.2 g/m^2/s of fuel for normal flames and 0.68 g/m^2/s of oxygen for inverse flames. This held across normal flames with ambient X_O2 0.20-0.38, burner X_fuel 0.13-1, total flow 0.6-12.2 mg/s and T_ad 2000-2800 K, and inverse flames with ambient X_C2H4 0.08-0.12, burner X_O2 0.40-0.85, 2.3-11.3 mg/s and T_ad 2080-2590 K.

At constant burner flow, the normal ethylene flames at 1 atm grew monotonically after ignition while their peak gas temperature generally fell. Burn times were 28-336 s. Radiative extinction occurred when the growing flame's radiative loss approached its chemical heat release. Just before total extinction, many flames entered an oscillatory mode, partially extinguishing and re-forming with growing amplitude.

ranking.one_line: Single drops of methanol and heptane were burned floating freely on the Space Station in air thinned with nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium, to find how little oxygen still lets a fuel burn in weightlessness and how well these gases put flames out; it also discovered that heptane drops keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame dies.

key_findings.claim: Limiting oxygen index in O2/N2: about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for n-heptane droplets. NASA describes the LOI found as significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted; the 2012 FLEX overview states microgravity flames burned at as much as 2-3 percent less oxygen (the source does not say whether relative or absolute). Consistent with this, the PSI table lists methanol tests that burned 5-11 s and extinguished at 0.12 O2 (8 tests) and heptane tests at 0.13 O2 that burned only 1.0-1.5 s with extinction diameter about equal to the initial diameter (transient burning below the LOI).

Carbon dioxide as suppressant: dispersing CO2 into 1 atm air raised the LOI to about 0.14 for methanol (0.14 O2/0.56 N2/0.30 CO2) and about 0.17 for heptane (0.17 O2/0.63 N2/0.20 CO2), i.e. roughly 30% and 20% CO2 by volume were needed to prevent quasi-steady burning of these fuels. The authors attribute the higher LOI to CO2's larger heat capacity (lower flame temperature) and its radiative participation. The PSI table shows methanol still burning 3.4-5.9 s at 0.14 O2 with 0.36 CO2, and heptane at 0.17 O2/0.20 CO2 extinguishing after 1.6-1.9 s with d_ext/d0 = 0.97.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station burned tiny gas jets in a gentle, adjustable air stream and turned the fuel up until each flame just started to give off smoke, to learn how air flow and burner size control soot release when there is no gravity.

key_findings.claim: Laminar smoke points exist for non-buoyant co-flowing jet flames, contrary to Glassman's 1988 prediction. On the ISS, 52 smoke points (final-report table: 6 ethylene, 6 propane, 20 propylene, 13 for 75% and 7 for 50% propylene; the same report's closing remarks say 55) were found at 0.41-1.6 mm burners and 5.4-65 cm/s co-flow. All smoke-point flames were attached, with Re 36-788.

For a given fuel and burner, raising the co-flow velocity lengthens the smoke point, even though at fixed fuel flow it shortens the luminous flame. Example (pure propylene, 1.6 mm burner, smoke-point review sheet): L_SP rose from about 14.0 mm at u_a = 9.1 cm/s to 25.7 mm at 51.4 cm/s. The investigators attribute this to decreased residence times and radiative losses as co-flow velocity increases.

ranking.one_line: The follow-on to FLEX burned single drops and pairs of drops of practical-fuel ingredients and fuel mixtures (octanes, heptane, decane, alcohols) on the Space Station to give engine and fire modellers clean benchmark data, and showed that the 'cool flames' found in FLEX occur for many normal-alkane fuels.

key_findings.claim: Cool-flame (second-stage) burning after hot-flame radiative extinction occurs for several n-alkanes, not only heptane: n-heptane, n-octane and n-decane droplets in O2/N2/CO2 and O2/He/N2 at 0.5, 0.7 and 1 atm (14-25% O2) showed quasi-steady low-temperature burning, cool-flame extinction at a finite diameter and vapour-cloud formation, while smaller droplets burned to completion or disrupted. Cool-flame extinction diameters of the three alkanes followed a trend resembling their ignition delay times.

n-Decane at 0.5 atm in O2/N2: a 4.03 mm droplet in air burned with K = 0.41 mm2/s in the hot-flame stage (visible extinction at ~14.6 s) and 0.33 mm2/s in the cool-flame stage, whose end was marked by a drop in the narrowband radiometer signal; at 25% O2 a 3.79 mm droplet avoided radiative extinction and micro-exploded at 26 s (K = 0.52 mm2/s); at 17% and 14% O2 hot/cool K were 0.31/0.27 and 0.29/0.25 mm2/s with earlier extinctions.

pressure_kpa.note: reported for film tests; about 1 atm overall

ranking.one_line: Astronauts ran 129 burns of small plastic and fabric samples in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS while lowering the oxygen with nitrogen, to find the weakest airflow and the lowest oxygen at which solids keep burning without gravity, and to compare that with the Earth test NASA uses to approve materials.

key_findings.claim: Bhattacharjee, thin PMMA films in opposed flow at about 21% O2: flames went out by radiative extinction as the flow was lowered. This happened at about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 um films and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 um (1-2 cm wide, about 1 atm). Within the large uncertainty of flow calibration at such low speeds, the extinction velocity does not depend on thickness, although the spread rate does. A 2-D model gave 1.5 cm/s for all four thicknesses. Approaching extinction, the flame shrank and turned from orange to all blue within about 3 s. With the flow cut off completely, a 100 um flame spreading at 2.2 mm/s went out within 2 s.

Bhattacharjee: across opposed flows from about 40 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s in microgravity, the highest spread rate over 100 um PMMA (2 cm wide, about 20.7-21% O2) was 2.2 mm/s. This is about the same as the 2.0 mm/s measured for downward spread in 1 g air on the same fuel, and the flame shapes were similar. The authors conclude that downward spread over PMMA at 21% O2 on Earth is thermally controlled with little kinetic effect. Applying the de Ris thin-fuel formula to the 2.2 mm/s maximum spread rate for 100 um film gives F = 4.76. Combined with 1 g thick-fuel data (0.044 mm/s), this gives an effective buoyant opposed velocity of 1.9 cm/s and a thin/thick transition thickness of 5.2 mm for downward spread in air.

ranking.one_line: Nine strip-shaped samples of spacecraft materials were set alight inside an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit to see whether they burn more or less readily than in NASA's standard ground flammability test; silicone and Nomex would not burn in weightlessness, while a cotton-fibreglass fabric and thick acrylic burned but with flames that stopped growing.

key_findings.claim: No flame spread on silicone in microgravity. None of the four silicone sheets (0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm concurrent; 0.37 mm opposed; 20 cm/s air, about 22.1% O2; the PSI table lists sample 2-1 at about 21.5% while the published Table I (NTRS 20170008805) gives about 22.1%) propagated. ranking.one_line: On the Space Station, small pieces of common spacecraft materials (Teflon, Kapton, silicone rubber, cotton lamp wick) were overheated without burning, and the size of the smoke particles was measured to find out what kind of smoke detector would reliably catch an early spacecraft fire.

key_findings.claim: Fresh (unaged) smoke from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity was sub-micrometre in number terms. Final-report values (geometric mean / count mean / diameter of average mass, nm; sigma_g): Kapton 80/105/179, 2.08; lamp wick 186/227/341, 1.89; silicone rubber 189/257/472, 2.18; Teflon 170/205/297, 1.84.

Holding the smoke for 720 s raised all mean sizes and narrowed the distribution, consistent with coagulation. Geometric mean diameter rose to 155 nm (Kapton, x1.9), 258 nm (lamp wick, x1.4), 352 nm (silicone, x1.9) and 228 nm (Teflon, x1.3). Diameter of average mass rose by 28-49%, to 267-606 nm, and sigma_g fell to 1.81-1.83 for all four materials. During aging the P-Trak number count fell substantially while DustTrak mass stayed nearly constant, which indicates coagulation with little wall loss.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts burned small fabric strips, plastic spheres and slabs, and wax candles in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS to see whether solids burn more readily without gravity than in the Earth-based test NASA uses to approve materials, and whether a puff of nitrogen puts the flames out.

key_findings.claim: In opposed flow in microgravity (2-cm-wide SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric, ISS air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), the flame reached steady spread within seconds of each flow change. Spread rate rose with flow to a maximum at about 10-15 cm/s and fell at higher speeds.

The same SIBAL fabric cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) spread in 1 g air: it ignites, then extinguishes, because the buoyant flow exceeds the blow-off limit. In microgravity at about 9-10 cm/s opposed flow it burned steadily over the whole sample. For this fabric and geometry, it is more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g, which supports the BASS hypothesis.

D_avm rose from 0.106 to 0.169 um (Kapton), 0.271 to 0.401 um (lampwick), 0.468 to 0.628 um (silicone) and 0.377 to 0.529 um (Pyrell), and sigma_g fell to 1.67-1.96. Teflon was the exception: Dg did not grow (0.093 to 0.080 um) and sigma_g widened to 2.34. Number counts fell by a factor of 1.7-2.7 over about 800 s. This agreed with coagulation theory within about 20% for number and 4% for D_avm, but sigma_g fell more than twice as much as predicted.

ranking.one_line: NASA lit a 94-cm-long sheet of cotton-fibreglass fabric inside an empty cargo spacecraft after it left the ISS, the first large fire deliberately set in orbit, to see whether a fire in microgravity keeps growing or settles to a steady size.

key_findings.claim: In concurrent flow at about 20 cm/s and 21.7% O2 (falling to 21.5%) near 1 atm, the flame over the 40.6 cm x 94 cm SIBAL sheet reached a steady state: it spread at a constant average 1.8 mm/s, and the flame length reached a plateau of about 40 mm. It burned about 84 cm of the 94 cm sheet during the 420 s allotted. On Earth the same configuration (upward burning) consumes the whole sample with an accelerating flame. This answers the main Saffire question: a large concurrent fire in microgravity, under forced ventilation, need not keep growing.

The opposed-flow flame (spreading into the 20 cm/s flow, ~21.5% O2) burned the remaining ~10 cm of fabric in about 70 s at an average 1.3 mm/s, with a flame length of about 24 mm. In 1 g this fabric does not spread downward (burn length ~0). So for this material, opposed-flow spread is possible in microgravity at a cabin-like ventilation speed but not on Earth. The concurrent flame spread about 1.4 times faster than the opposed flame.

ranking.one_line: Fuel droplets about 4 mm across were burned in a sealed chamber on the ISS to study 'cool flames': invisible, low-temperature flames (roughly 700-900 K) that keep a droplet burning after its normal hot flame has gone out.

key_findings.claim: With pure n-dodecane in air (21% O2, balance N2), droplets of about 3.8-4.7 mm at 0.5-1.25 atm burned first with a hot flame. The flame went out by radiative extinction after about 10-14 s (up to 17 s), with the droplet at about 2.9-4.3 mm. Quasi-steady cool-flame burning usually followed, often ending with a large vapour cloud. Not every test shows this: FLEX-1207 to 1210 have no cool-flame extinction diameter, the FLEX-1207 comment notes no large vapour cloud, and the FLEX-1222 comment says the flame burned to completion. The cool-flame burning-rate constant (0.31-0.43 mm^2/s) was about the same as the hot-flame value (0.30-0.52 mm^2/s).

For n-dodecane in air the cool-flame extinction diameter falls steeply with pressure. It was 1.73-1.92 mm at 0.5 atm (50.7 kPa; 5 tests), 0.68-1.14 mm at 0.75 atm (76 kPa; 5 tests), mostly 0.26-0.85 mm at 1 atm (101 kPa; one outlier of 2.97 mm in FLEX-1251), and 0-0.39 mm at 1.25 atm (127 kPa). At 2-5 atm most droplets left no measurable residual droplet (recorded as 0 mm). The investigators note that simplified chemistry predicts these diameters less well as pressure rises.

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames on the Space Station were placed in a strong electric field between the burner and a metal mesh; the field drags the flame's natural ions and the gas around them, creating an adjustable 'ion wind' that can reshape, compact, de-soot or stabilise the flame with no buoyancy present.

key_findings.claim: First buoyancy-free mapping of ion-wind effects on flames: ISS tests ran March-November 2018 (20 test days, 219 flames) with methane and ethylene flames on coflow and gas-jet burners in fields of either polarity up to 10 kV, giving data on ion current and flame response without the confounding natural convection present in all ground tests.

In microgravity the voltage-current characteristic of methane coflow flames shows a distinct peak ion current at saturation, where the flame is most compact; beyond the saturation peak the current falls along a parabolic branch, unlike the 1 g plateau.

ranking.one_line: A repeat of the first large spacecraft fire experiment, with the air blowing a little faster, to see how ventilation speed changes how fast a large sheet of fabric burns in an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit.

key_findings.claim: Concurrent burn (S1) at about 25 cm/s and 21.2-21.0% O2, near 1 atm: the flame spread over about 84 cm of the 40.6-cm-wide sheet at an average 2.3 mm/s, burning for about 300 s (investigators' table; 320 s in the ASGSR slides). In 1 g the same configuration burns completely with an accelerating flame. Together with Saffire-I, the investigators conclude that concurrent spread over this thin fabric in microgravity reaches a steady rate and a limiting flame length.

Opposed burn (S2) at about 25 cm/s: the flame spread into the flow at 0.98 mm/s over about 10 cm in 60 s. This fabric does not spread downward in 1 g (burn length ~0). At 25 cm/s the concurrent flame spread 2.3 times faster than the opposed flame, against 1.4 times at 20 cm/s in Saffire-I.

ranking.one_line: Detailed computer models of single burning fuel droplets, checked against droplet fires on the Space Station, explain when a droplet flame drops into a dim, low-temperature 'cool flame', how long it survives, and why the gas xenon is a poor fire suppressant.

key_findings.claim: In 1 atm air with do of about 4 mm, n-heptane, n-decane and n-dodecane all show two-stage burning: a hot flame, radiative extinction, then quasi-steady cool-flame burning. The hot-to-cool transition happens at a nearly universal peak flame temperature of about 1200 K, and at transition the FSR and Tmax of the three fuels are almost identical.

Longer alkanes give more robust cool flames. Predicted cool-flame peak temperature is about 775 K for n-dodecane, 737 K for n-decane and 720 K for n-heptane, and the cool-flame burning rate rises in the same order. The cool-flame extinction diameter falls with chain length. At do = 4 mm in 1 atm air the model gives 0.95 mm (C7), 0.43 mm (C10) and about 0.25 mm (C12). FLEX measurements give 1.10-1.30 mm for C7 (do 3.3-3.9 mm), 0.66-1.32 mm for C10 and 0-0.50 mm for C12 (do 4.0-4.4 mm).

ranking.one_line: Before flying a smoke-measuring experiment, NASA checked on the Space Station that a commercial particle counter, which normally relies on gravity to recycle its alcohol, still counted particles correctly in weightlessness, and in doing so made the first measurement of how dusty the Station air is.

key_findings.claim: The modified P-Trak worked in microgravity. In all sessions (2005 and 2006, runs of about 8-39 min) it showed no alcohol flooding, optics obscuration, nozzle clogging or error codes. Readings rose from zero into the middle of the range and returned to zero on HEPA zero checks. This was the main failure mode the condenser modification was meant to prevent.

The P-Trak tracked a high-concentration aerosol (Velcro test, 4 Mar 2005). When the crew repeatedly separated Velcro at the inlet, it rose to several readings above 30,000 particles/cm3 (logged maximum 45,400) and fell back in a logical way. The DustTrak also responded but stayed below 10% of its range. These readings could not be tied quantitatively to individual Velcro separations.

ranking.one_line: A computer simulation of smoke forming from a hot, vapour-releasing sample in a slow air stream shows that, without gravity, smoke particles can grow larger than on Earth, which matters for how spacecraft smoke detectors are designed.

key_findings.claim: At the SAME flow speed (8 cm/s), the Earth-gravity size distribution sampled 26 L0 downstream (Case 1EG) has a single maximum near 5 um and no particles larger than about 40 um. The microgravity distribution (Case 1MG) is bimodal, with maxima near 5 um and 30 um, and a small fraction of particles approaching 100 um.

In Earth gravity, buoyancy deflects hot DBP vapour toward the cool (300 K) upper wall. The resulting peak nucleation rate is about 1e14 m-3 s-1, against about 1e12 m-3 s-1 in microgravity, where nucleation occurs only around the edge of the wake. Number densities near the upper wall approach 1e12 m-3, so terrestrial smoke has far more particles below 5 um.

ranking.one_line: University at Buffalo researchers built and tested fast computer models of flames spreading over solid fuels in weightlessness, checking them against Space Station burning tests, as a step toward predicting which spacecraft materials can burn at which oxygen levels and air speeds.

key_findings.claim: Building the flamelet manifolds from 1-D flames with a quasi-coupled fuel surface boundary (rather than a fixed fuel inlet) is critically important for capturing the spatial variation of mixture fraction along a pyrolysing fuel surface.

The coupled radiative FGMs reproduce the wide range of chemical states (intermediate species) of the detailed 2-D solution in most of the flow, but differ near the flame attachment (leading-edge) location, where flame-wall interaction before the fuel starts to burn and curved flame structure are not represented by 1-D flamelets.

ranking.one_line: A ground study at Princeton, prompted by the surprising cool flames seen around burning droplets on the Space Station, used ozone-assisted counterflow burners and simulations to map when hot flames turn into low-temperature 'cool' and 'warm' flames and when those go out.

key_findings.claim: Without ozone, cool diffusion flames of larger n-alkanes survive at much leaner fuel loading: at similar strain rates, n-tetradecane cool flames extinguished at Yf = 0.322 (a = 82.6 1/s) whereas n-heptane needed Yf = 0.555 (a = 78.2 1/s); over the data set, cool-flame extinction Yf ranges 0.23-0.39 for n-C14 versus 0.50-0.56 for n-C7. The authors conclude the larger n-alkanes are substantially more reactive in the low-temperature regime.

Ozone addition to the oxidiser strongly enhances cool flames and nearly removes the fuel-size effect: with ozone, cool flames extinguished at Yf = 0.107 (n-C14, a = 69.1 1/s) and 0.109 (n-C7, a = 68.5 1/s), and the whole ozone data set spans Yf 0.044-0.22, i.e. roughly a third (n-C14) to a fifth (n-C7) of the fuel loading needed without ozone.

notes: Score = weighted mean of four components in [0, 1]: conditions (closeness of the nearest test to the scenario's O2, pressure and flow), material (fuel-phase transfer), pillar and evidence strength. Weights and scales are in fif/api.py and docs/methods.md; they are a judgement, shown so it can be argued with.

A distance of 1 means one scale step away: 3 points of O2, 15 kPa or 10 cm/s. A condition that was not recorded counts as far away as the farthest investigation that did record it (at least 2 steps); cabin-air experiments without logged O2 or pressure are placed at the nominal cabin atmosphere (listed in conditions_assumed_cabin_air).

A condition with no per-test value is read from the investigation's range (conditions_from_range or conditions_assumed_cabin_air; range and origin in condition_ranges); a wide range lowers the conditions score by 20%. A value shown for a column in a test's `not_measured` is the middle of a narrow range, not a reading of that test.
No PSI combustion test was run at partial gravity (0.38 g). The gravity component only rewards investigations that compare microgravity with 1 g, which brackets partial gravity.

fuel_phase weights the ranking, it does not filter it: an investigation on another fuel phase keeps its place with a lower material component and `phase_match` false. `nearest_test` is always a gas-fuel test (null when the investigation ran none); the test of another phase that its conditions score and distance come from is in `nearest_test_other_phase`.

Gap: the closest gas-fuel test to this scenario is PSI-23 19308 (methane, O2 0.300, 106 kPa not measured, middle of the range 101-110), 3.25 scale steps away. Conclusions for this scenario are extrapolations.

ranking.one_line: A flat gas burner on the Space Station imitated small burning patches of plastics and liquids in still air, showing that such flames can burn steadily for minutes without any air flow when oxygen is raised to about 26.5% or more, but go out within tens of seconds at 21%.

key_findings.claim: Small (25 mm) emulated condensed-fuel flames burned quasi-steadily for minutes in quiescent microgravity, with no air flow and no flame spread; more than half of round-1 tests (59 analysed ignitions) burned at least 2 and up to 5 minutes, and ~29 flames reached an apparently steady state for 120 s or more before shutdown.

Oxygen threshold for the 25 mm ethylene/N2 flames tested: all flames in 21% O2 (by volume) self-extinguished within 40 s, whereas steady flames were observed at nominal 26.5%, 34% and 40% O2. NASA's summary places the self-extinction boundary at roughly 25% O2. This is a threshold for these burner conditions (flow rates, sizes), not a material flammability limit.

ranking.one_line: Ground-commanded tests on the ISS burned ethane, propane and butane on a pea-sized porous sphere, both normally (fuel out of the sphere into an oxygen/nitrogen atmosphere) and inside-out (an oxygen-rich stream of up to 85% O2 out of the sphere into a fuel-filled chamber), and found the first spherical 'cool flames' of gaseous fuel.

key_findings.claim: Fifteen spherical cool diffusion flames of a gaseous fuel were observed, the first such observation. All followed radiative extinction of a hot flame, after a dark interval of 0.7-1.1 s. The cool flames of four tests in June 2021 (21174 C3, C4, C6, F1) were quasi-steady for about 14 s and disappeared when the fuel flow stopped; in one test the radiometer and burner temperature were steady enough to suggest the cool flame would have lasted indefinitely. The ten cool flames of tests 21291 A1 and C1 instead ended by re-igniting into hot flames.

Cool flames formed in a narrow window only: normal (not inverse) flames, n-butane (not ethane or propane) at 30% in N2 in the burner stream, flowing at 0.75-1.5 mg/s into 0.385-0.399 ambient O2 at 2.03 bar (about 203 kPa). Burner temperature also had to be above 515 K. None were seen below about 0.4 O2, below 2 bar, or for any inverse flame, including those fed with 85% O2.

ranking.one_line: On the space station, small ball-shaped flames of ethylene gas were burned for minutes around a porous sphere, either as fuel blowing into oxygen-rich air or as oxygen blowing into a fuel atmosphere, to learn when such flames make soot and when they go out.

key_findings.claim: At about 1 atm, every ethylene spherical flame that extinguished radiatively did so at a peak temperature of about 1130 K. The reactant mass flux through the flame sphere at extinction was about 0.2 g/m^2/s of fuel for normal flames and 0.68 g/m^2/s of oxygen for inverse flames. This held across normal flames with ambient X_O2 0.20-0.38, burner X_fuel 0.13-1, total flow 0.6-12.2 mg/s and T_ad 2000-2800 K, and inverse flames with ambient X_C2H4 0.08-0.12, burner X_O2 0.40-0.85, 2.3-11.3 mg/s and T_ad 2080-2590 K.

At constant burner flow, the normal ethylene flames at 1 atm grew monotonically after ignition while their peak gas temperature generally fell. Burn times were 28-336 s. Radiative extinction occurred when the growing flame's radiative loss approached its chemical heat release. Just before total extinction, many flames entered an oscillatory mode, partially extinguishing and re-forming with growing amplitude.

ranking.one_line: Single drops of methanol and heptane were burned floating freely on the Space Station in air thinned with nitrogen, carbon dioxide or helium, to find how little oxygen still lets a fuel burn in weightlessness and how well these gases put flames out; it also discovered that heptane drops keep burning with an invisible 'cool flame' after the visible flame dies.

key_findings.claim: Limiting oxygen index in O2/N2: about 0.12 for methanol and 0.15 for n-heptane droplets. NASA describes the LOI found as significantly lower than in normal gravity and lower than predicted; the 2012 FLEX overview states microgravity flames burned at as much as 2-3 percent less oxygen (the source does not say whether relative or absolute). Consistent with this, the PSI table lists methanol tests that burned 5-11 s and extinguished at 0.12 O2 (8 tests) and heptane tests at 0.13 O2 that burned only 1.0-1.5 s with extinction diameter about equal to the initial diameter (transient burning below the LOI).

Carbon dioxide as suppressant: dispersing CO2 into 1 atm air raised the LOI to about 0.14 for methanol (0.14 O2/0.56 N2/0.30 CO2) and about 0.17 for heptane (0.17 O2/0.63 N2/0.20 CO2), i.e. roughly 30% and 20% CO2 by volume were needed to prevent quasi-steady burning of these fuels. The authors attribute the higher LOI to CO2's larger heat capacity (lower flame temperature) and its radiative participation. The PSI table shows methanol still burning 3.4-5.9 s at 0.14 O2 with 0.36 CO2, and heptane at 0.17 O2/0.20 CO2 extinguishing after 1.6-1.9 s with d_ext/d0 = 0.97.

ranking.one_line: On the space station, gas fuels (hydrogen, methane, ethylene, diluted with nitrogen or helium) were fed out of a small porous ball into still oxygen-containing gas to make nearly perfect spherical flames, to see how such flames grow, and how they go out when the fuel supply is too small or when the flame becomes so large that it loses too much heat by radiation.

key_findings.claim: For nitrogen-diluted ethylene in air (20% C2H4/80% N2 fuel stream, ~21% O2, ~1 atm), a flow of 3 cc/s produced a quasi-steady spherical flame that lasted until the automated system stopped it at the 250 C burner limit. At 5-10 cc/s the same mixture's flames grew until radiative extinction. Mixtures of 25% and 30% C2H4 also showed radiative extinction at the higher flows.

Radiative extinction of growing spherical diffusion flames, predicted computationally but never conclusively seen in 2.2 s or 5 s drop towers or on parabolic aircraft, turned out to be a common event on the ISS. Kinetic extinction could also be reached only because a near-steady flame could be established first and then ramped down. The investigators list it first among the flight's initial surprises and discoveries.

pressure_kpa.note: reported for film tests; about 1 atm overall

ranking.one_line: Astronauts ran 129 burns of small plastic and fabric samples in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS while lowering the oxygen with nitrogen, to find the weakest airflow and the lowest oxygen at which solids keep burning without gravity, and to compare that with the Earth test NASA uses to approve materials.

key_findings.claim: Bhattacharjee, thin PMMA films in opposed flow at about 21% O2: flames went out by radiative extinction as the flow was lowered. This happened at about 1 cm/s for 100, 200 and 300 um films and about 1.5 cm/s for 400 um (1-2 cm wide, about 1 atm). Within the large uncertainty of flow calibration at such low speeds, the extinction velocity does not depend on thickness, although the spread rate does. A 2-D model gave 1.5 cm/s for all four thicknesses. Approaching extinction, the flame shrank and turned from orange to all blue within about 3 s. With the flow cut off completely, a 100 um flame spreading at 2.2 mm/s went out within 2 s.

Bhattacharjee: across opposed flows from about 40 cm/s down to about 1 cm/s in microgravity, the highest spread rate over 100 um PMMA (2 cm wide, about 20.7-21% O2) was 2.2 mm/s. This is about the same as the 2.0 mm/s measured for downward spread in 1 g air on the same fuel, and the flame shapes were similar. The authors conclude that downward spread over PMMA at 21% O2 on Earth is thermally controlled with little kinetic effect. Applying the de Ris thin-fuel formula to the 2.2 mm/s maximum spread rate for 100 um film gives F = 4.76. Combined with 1 g thick-fuel data (0.044 mm/s), this gives an effective buoyant opposed velocity of 1.9 cm/s and a thin/thick transition thickness of 5.2 mm for downward spread in air.

ranking.one_line: Nine strip-shaped samples of spacecraft materials were set alight inside an empty cargo spacecraft in orbit to see whether they burn more or less readily than in NASA's standard ground flammability test; silicone and Nomex would not burn in weightlessness, while a cotton-fibreglass fabric and thick acrylic burned but with flames that stopped growing.

key_findings.claim: No flame spread on silicone in microgravity. None of the four silicone sheets (0.27, 0.61 and 1.03 mm concurrent; 0.37 mm opposed; 20 cm/s air, about 22.1% O2; the PSI table lists sample 2-1 at about 21.5% while the published Table I (NTRS 20170008805) gives about 22.1%) propagated. After the 9.2 s, 80 W igniter switched off, a tiny gas-phase flame remained briefly, did not spread and went out. Burn time was 'insignificant' and microgravity burn length about 0 for all four.

Silicone was less flammable in microgravity than in the 1-g test. In 1-g tests on matching samples, the 0.27 mm silicone burned completely with accelerating upward spread, the 0.61 mm burned on average 7.6 cm of 30 cm (1.2 mm/s) and the 1.03 mm did not burn. The 0.37 mm sheet burned completely downward at 0.6 mm/s. Published 1-g Test 1 minimum oxygen concentrations (MOC; the term used by the cited source) for silicone are 18% (0.25 mm), 20% (0.61 mm) and 22% (1.00 mm), so the roughly 22.1% O2 flight atmosphere was at or above the 1-g MOC for every thickness. The investigators conclude silicone flammability in microgravity is reduced compared with 1 g, at least at 20 cm/s. This was unexpected: cellulose and PMMA experience suggested that a material that burns upward in 1 g would also burn in microgravity at moderate flow.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts burned small fabric strips, plastic spheres and slabs, and wax candles in a gentle, adjustable air stream on the ISS to see whether solids burn more readily without gravity than in the Earth-based test NASA uses to approve materials, and whether a puff of nitrogen puts the flames out.

key_findings.claim: In opposed flow in microgravity (2-cm-wide SIBAL cotton-fibreglass fabric, ISS air, about 21-22% O2, about 1 atm), the flame reached steady spread within seconds of each flow change. Spread rate rose with flow to a maximum at about 10-15 cm/s and fell at higher speeds.

The same SIBAL fabric cannot sustain downward (opposed-flow) spread in 1 g air: it ignites, then extinguishes, because the buoyant flow exceeds the blow-off limit. In microgravity at about 9-10 cm/s opposed flow it burned steadily over the whole sample. For this fabric and geometry, it is more flammable in microgravity than in 1 g, which supports the BASS hypothesis.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station burned tiny gas jets in a gentle, adjustable air stream and turned the fuel up until each flame just started to give off smoke, to learn how air flow and burner size control soot release when there is no gravity.

key_findings.claim: Laminar smoke points exist for non-buoyant co-flowing jet flames, contrary to Glassman's 1988 prediction. On the ISS, 52 smoke points (final-report table: 6 ethylene, 6 propane, 20 propylene, 13 for 75% and 7 for 50% propylene; the same report's closing remarks say 55) were found at 0.41-1.6 mm burners and 5.4-65 cm/s co-flow. All smoke-point flames were attached, with Re 36-788.

For a given fuel and burner, raising the co-flow velocity lengthens the smoke point, even though at fixed fuel flow it shortens the luminous flame. Example (pure propylene, 1.6 mm burner, smoke-point review sheet): L_SP rose from about 14.0 mm at u_a = 9.1 cm/s to 25.7 mm at 51.4 cm/s. The investigators attribute this to decreased residence times and radiative losses as co-flow velocity increases.

ranking.one_line: Astronauts on the Space Station photographed small gas flames burning from a tube into a gentle stream of air, to see how flames lift off, hold on and make soot without gravity and to provide test cases for computer models of flames.

key_findings.claim: Microgravity made a sooting methane flame larger, sootier and cooler. For a 100% CH4 flame on the 3.23 mm nozzle (mean fuel velocity 46 cm/s, nominal coflow 18 cm/s), the microgravity flame was taller and wider than its 1-g counterpart. Its peak soot volume fraction was about 8 times higher, and its peak soot temperature about 200 K lower because of the larger radiative loss.

The model predicted flame shape and soot location but not the microgravity soot increase. The sectional soot model reproduced the 1-g to microgravity change in flame shape and the shift of soot to the wings. It gave the right order of magnitude for 1-g soot but did not capture the eightfold rise in microgravity. The investigators suspect the optically thin radiation assumption (no reabsorption).

ranking.one_line: Small methane and ethylene flames surrounded by a gentle co-flowing air stream were burned on the Space Station, from very diluted near-extinction flames to very sooty ones, to give computer models clean, buoyancy-free benchmark data; the sooty flames held several times more soot than on Earth and diluted flames survived at lower fuel concentrations.

key_findings.claim: SLICE precursor (N2-diluted CH4, mole fraction 0.4-1.0, mean inlet velocity 23-90 cm/s): luminous flame length is proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow in both 1 g and microgravity, microgravity flames are noticeably longer, dilution has negligible effect on shape once normalised by methane flow, and buoyancy narrows 1 g flames through radially inward convection near the flame front.

Campaign scope from the PSI table: 344 flames on 32 test days across three ISS rounds (methane Nov 2017-Feb 2018, 130 flames; ethylene May-Sept 2018, 162 flames; 'improved coflow tests' Feb-Mar 2021, 52 flames), with 2 to 18 flames per day.
